answer:
Analysis complete. All four refinements are bound and applied; deliverables written to `analysis/`.

═══════════════════════════════════════
FINAL HYPOTHESIS
═══════════════════════════════════════
Across the only three wealth waves available in this file — **1985, 1990 and 1996** — with **1985 the earliest wealth measurement**, so "from 1985 onwards" is bounded by these three waves, respondents in the **white** cohort (racial/ethnic cohort 3 = NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC, a label that also contains the small Asian, Native American and other groups NLSY79 does not separate) held **higher median family net wealth than black (cohort 1) and Hispanic (cohort 2) respondents at every wave, and the gap widened substantially in both absolute and relative terms.** In nominal dollars exactly as recorded: in **1985** the white median was **$3,500** versus **$1,600 for black** respondents (gap $1,900; ratio 2.2×) and **$500 for Hispanic** respondents (gap $3,000; ratio 7.0× — a figure to read only with caution, since that median is below $1,000 and **41.9% of Hispanic respondents were at or below zero net wealth**, so the level gap is the reliable statement); in **1990** the white median was **$12,972** versus **$4,800 black** (gap $8,172; 2.7×) and **$1,600 Hispanic** (gap $11,372; 8.1×); in **1996** the white median was **$42,600** versus **$9,800 black** (gap $32,800; 4.4×) and **$2,562 Hispanic** (gap $40,038; 16.6×). The white-to-black ratio roughly **doubled (2.2 → 4.4)** and the white-to-Hispanic ratio rose from **about 7 to about 17**, and the widening is not an artefact of inflation: in constant 1996 dollars (deflators from CPI-U annual averages, 1982–84 = 100, 1985 = 107.6, 1990 = 130.7, 1996 = 156.9, i.e. ×1.458 and ×1.200) the white–black gap grew from ≈**$2,771 to $32,800** and the white–Hispanic gap from ≈**$4,375 to $40,038**, because real median wealth rose about **8.4-fold for whites versus 4.2-fold for blacks and 3.5-fold for Hispanics**. The ordering white > black > Hispanic is stable at all three waves, but the groups' distributions overlap heavily — in 1996 the white 25th percentile ($8,500) sits *below* the black median ($9,800) — so the difference is a shift in central tendency and in the share holding no or negative net wealth (1996: 10.9% white, 20.8% black, 34.9% Hispanic) rather than a clean separation between groups; the same pattern holds in the balanced panel of 5,739 respondents observed in all three waves (1996 ratios 4.7 and 17.8), so it is not produced by available-case estimation. This comparison is purely descriptive, and it is materially qualified because the wealth variables are a **family-level** measure (respondent/spouse assets minus debts) assigned to individual respondents who were only 20–28 years old in 1985, so part of the early gap may reflect differences in family formation and marriage rather than individual wealth accumulation, and because all estimates are **unweighted and computed on all cases available per wave**, with the balanced-panel figures serving as the sensitivity check.

═══════════════════════════════════════
EVIDENCE — 1. PRIMARY: available cases per wave (nominal $)
═══════════════════════════════════════
| Wave | Cohort | n | Median | 95% CI | Mean | Q1 | Q3 | % ≤0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | white (NBNH) | 5,774 | **3,500** | 3,200–3,700 | 15,201 | 500 | 11,750 | 19.2 |
| 1985 | black | 1,699 | **1,600** | 1,480–1,800 | 7,728 | 0 | 5,700 | 28.4 |
| 1985 | Hispanic | 2,631 | **500** | 400–600 | 4,919 | 0 | 3,022 | 41.9 |
| 1990 | white (NBNH) | 5,336 | **12,972** | 11,899–13,700 | 52,387 | 1,665 | 44,738 | 16.5 |
| 1990 | black | 1,528 | **4,800** | 4,000–5,450 | 27,220 | 0 | 21,525 | 25.5 |
| 1990 | Hispanic | 2,431 | **1,600** | 1,400–2,000 | 13,394 | 0 | 8,200 | 33.8 |
| 1996 | white (NBNH) | 3,557 | **42,600** | 40,500–46,000 | 114,352 | 8,500 | 114,500 | 10.9 |
| 1996 | black | 1,368 | **9,800** | 8,300–11,600 | 45,080 | 1,000 | 45,500 | 20.8 |
| 1996 | Hispanic | 2,114 | **2,562** | 2,000–3,000 | 22,213 | 0 | 17,495 | 34.9 |

IQRs (= Q3−Q1) are in the table file. **Refinement 2 checked explicitly: all 9 cohort-wave medians are strictly positive — none is ≤ 0** — but the Hispanic 1985 median ($500) is below $1,000 with 41.9% at or below zero, so I flagged it `UNSTABLE (denominator median < $1,000)` and led with the $3,000 level gap, giving the 7.0× ratio only with that caveat. Means are 4–6× the medians everywhere, so they are reported for context only and never used for claims (see limitation on top-coding below).

═══════════════════════════════════════
EVIDENCE — 2. Gaps & ratios (nominal $; bootstrap B=2,000)
═══════════════════════════════════════
| Wave | Contrast | Median gap | Gap 95% CI | Ratio | Ratio 95% CI |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | white vs black | +1,900 | 1,500–2,200 | 2.19 | 1.82–2.49 |
| 1985 | white vs Hispanic | +3,000 | 2,700–3,211 | 7.00 ⚠ | 5.75–8.75 |
| 1990 | white vs black | +8,172 | 6,892–9,233 | 2.70 | 2.34–3.27 |
| 1990 | white vs Hispanic | +11,372 | 10,125–12,150 | 8.11 | 6.35–9.29 |
| 1996 | white vs black | +32,800 | 30,200–36,470 | 4.35 | 3.67–5.24 |
| 1996 | white vs Hispanic | +40,038 | 37,899–43,200 | 16.62 | 13.80–21.30 |

⚠ = flagged unstable per refinement 2. Gap CIs exclude zero in all six cells.

═══════════════════════════════════════
EVIDENCE — 3. Secondary: constant 1996$ (deflators ×1.458 / ×1.200 / ×1.000)
═══════════════════════════════════════
white 5,104 → 15,572 → 42,600 (**×8.35**); black 2,333 → 5,762 → 9,800 (**×4.20**); Hispanic 729 → 1,921 → 2,562 (**×3.51**). Real white–black gap 2,771 → 9,810 → 32,800; real white–Hispanic gap 4,375 → 13,652 → 40,038. Used only for the widened/narrowed claim, per refinement 1; the deflator values are stated in the hypothesis itself.

═══════════════════════════════════════
EVIDENCE — 4. Sensitivity: balanced panel (n=5,739, 45.2%)
═══════════════════════════════════════
| Wave | white | black | Hispanic | W/B | W/H |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | 3,800 | 1,600 | 300 | 2.38 | 12.67 |
| 1990 | 14,750 | 4,100 | 1,200 | 3.60 | 12.29 |
| 1996 | 42,600 | 9,075 | 2,400 | 4.69 | 17.75 |

**Honest correction to my pre-analysis expectation:** I predicted the balanced panel would *shrink* the gap because whites were lost fastest (52.6% missing by 1996 vs 31.7% black). It does not — ratios are similar or slightly larger at every wave, so the widening is not an artefact of differential attrition or available-case estimation.

═══════════════════════════════════════
VERIFICATION & CAVEATS
═══════════════════════════════════════
• Every headline median was **re-derived through an independent code path** (`groupby(...).median()` vs the helper functions) and matched exactly: 3,500/1,600/500; 12,972/4,800/1,600; 42,600/9,800/2,562.5. The 1996 white median 42,600 is a genuine observed value, not interpolation.
• Refinement 3's Kruskal–Wallis is reported in RESULTS.md **with** the required caveat: H = 625.9 / 737.5 / 1,080.9, p < 1e-100, but the file carries no weights and no strata/PSU identifiers, so these p-values and the bootstrap CIs reflect **within-file sampling noise only** for an unweighted, non-nationally-representative tabulation with deliberately oversampled black and Hispanic cohorts.
• Overlap check performed: white Q1 lies below the black median in all three waves, so no median should be read as group separation.
• Top-coding carried through as a limitation, not silently: the source caps the top (2.0% of 1996 obs sit exactly at 1,232,183; 3.49% of whites vs 0.66% of blacks), so means/upper tails are understated — medians fall far below the cap and are unaffected.
• Zeros retained (verified genuine: 96.8% of the 1,497 zero-wealth cases have all four component assets 0/null); no bottom winsorizing.

Deliverables: `analysis/RESULTS.md` (tidy median/gap/ratio tables, real-$ table, sensitivity, overlap), `analysis/wealth_medians_by_race.csv`, `analysis/ratio_and_gap_uncertainty.csv`, and the three executed scripts.

Remaining limitations: the family-vs-individual mismatch (no household ID or marital-status column exists in the file, so it cannot be tested, only disclosed); "white" is an imposed label on NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC; race is fixed at 1979; the 1990→1996 step spans six years, not five; and the cohort ages 20–28 → 32–40 over the window, so these are cohort life-cycle wealth profiles, not population wealth.

payload.workflow: 1) Input inspection (analysis/01_inspect_inputs.py): confirmed 12,686 unique respondents x 61 columns; located the three wealth columns ('Family net wealth, 1985', 'Family net wealth, 1990', 'Family net wealth, 1996 (key data point)') and 'Racial/ethnic cohort, 1979' (1=BLACK 2,002, 2=HISPANIC 3,174, 3=NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC 7,510, no missing, no sentinel codes); documented missingness (20.4%/26.7%/44.5% overall, differential by cohort), severe right skew (mean/median 4.4-6.1), mass at or below zero (26.7%/22.5%/20.0%), source top-coding at each wave's maximum, and that $0 wealth is genuine (96.8% of zero cases have all component assets 0/null). 2) Main analysis (analysis/02_wealth_by_race.py): cohort 3 mapped to 'white'; zeros and negatives retained; per wave x cohort computed n, mean, Q1, median, Q3, IQR, share<=0 with 2,000-replicate percentile bootstrap 95% CIs on medians; white-minus-X dollar gaps and white/X median ratios computed within wave (so deflator-invariant); nominal dollars primary with constant-1996$ secondary (CPI-U 107.6/130.7/156.9); primary estimand = all available cases per wave, sensitivity = balanced panel of respondents with wealth in all three waves; Kruskal-Wallis computed but reported only under an explicit no-weights/no-strata caveat. 3) Ratio-uncertainty check (analysis/03_ratio_uncertainty.py): bootstrap CIs for all six ratios and gaps, with an explicit instability flag where the denominator median is below $1,000 (Hispanic 1985). 4) Verification: all nine medians independently re-derived through a second code path (groupby-median) and matched exactly; outputs written to analysis/RESULTS.md, wealth_medians_by_race.csv, ratio_and_gap_uncertainty.csv.
